title: Graceful burst absorption: GPU reservoir controller and KV affinity throttling
creator: Aisha Patel
description: High QPS bursts cause transient GPU memory pressure: large inflight microbatches plus KV cache allocations lead to kernel failures or aggressive KV eviction. This ticket implements a runtime-level 'GPU reservoir controller' that maintains a dynamically sized headroom reservoir and an affinity-based throttling policy for requests likely to increase KV working set. The goal is graceful absorption of short bursts without sacrificing steady-state throughput.
background: Recent incidents (see ENG-7421, ENG-83100) show that short high-QPS spikes produce two failure modes: 1) Kernel OOMs when microbatch growth exceeds available GPU headroom, and 2) aggressive KV eviction causing cache thrashing and latency regressions. Existing admission control uses simple queue-length heuristics; it doesn't account for per-request KV affinity or reserved headroom for KV growth during a burst.
goals: Prevent GPU OOMs during bursts by reserving flexible headroom on each worker
Reduce KV cache thrashing by prioritizing requests with high cache hit probability
Preserve p50/p95 latency SLOs for steady traffic while absorbing short spikes
Provide observability and tuning knobs for operations teams (reservoir targets, affinity thresholds)
success_metrics: p95 generation latency increase <= 10% during 1-minute 3x QPS bursts compared to baseline
< 1 kernel OOM per 10M requests over 30d in affected pools
KV eviction rate decrease by 30% during bursts vs current behavior
No regression in steady-state throughput beyond 5%
approach: Two complementary runtime components: (A) GPU reservoir controller: a per-GPU memory allocator that keeps a flexible 'reservoir' (headroom) calculated from recent variance in microbatch allocations, expected KV growth, and emergency margin. The controller exposes a fast admission token that microbatch allocator consults. (B) KV-affinity throttler: a lightweight classifier that tags incoming requests with a 'kv-affinity score' (based on model id, input prefix hash, user id hotness) and prefers admitting low-affinity requests when headroom is low. For high-affinity requests the controller can: delay by a bounded window (50-200ms), route to a lower-capacity reserved queue, or fall back to a high-quantization model variant.
design_decisions: Reservoir sizing uses EWMA of recent peak memory consumption plus a percentile-based safety multiplier instead of static fixed thresholds
Affinity score computed with a rolling count sketch (approx count-min) to keep memory overhead small and avoid per-key state explosion
Admission outcomes are categorical: admit, delay (soft-throttle), degrade (route to quantized model), or drop — mapped to operator-configurable policies
Controller runs entirely in the serving process to avoid cross-process coordination latency; a gossip sync provides rough cluster-level headroom signals for heavy multislot workloads
Telemetry: emit reservoir_free, reservoir_target, kv_affinity_score, admission_decision, and microbatch_size_histogram to existing console dashboards
implementation_tasks: Prototype reservoir controller in runtime main loop (C++) with a feature flag
Implement affinity scorer using existing prefix-hash utilities; add sketch-based counters (lightweight) to worker hot path
Modify microbatch allocator to consult controller before expanding batch slots; add bounded delay queue with exponential backoff jitter
Add policy config (reservoir_target_pct, affinity_thresholds, delay_ms_range, degrade_route) to runtime config and console UI
Instrument metrics and traces; add logs for admission decision including reason codes
Create unit tests for controller logic and integration tests with synthetic QPS bursts in the perf harness
Open PRs, performance benchmarks, and update runbooks
testing_plan: Unit tests for reservoir arithmetic (EWMA + percentile) with deterministic sequences
Fuzz tests for affinity scorer to validate no high-cost paths in hot loop
End-to-end perf tests in the CI perf harness: 0.5x/1x/3x/5x baseline QPS bursts with mixed affinity distribution
Chaos test: simulate worker GPU memory pressure and ensure controller prevents kernel OOMs and triggers degrade/delay policies
Canary rollout in a single region with 10% traffic and automated rollback if p95 latency > baseline+15% or kernel OOMs observed
rollout_plan: Feature-flagged beta: enable on dev clusters and run synthetic burst suite (2 weeks)
Internal canary: rollout to runtime-qa and one low-traffic prod cluster (2 days), monitor dashboards
Gradual roll: increase to 30%/60%/100% over 1 week with automated SLO gates
Operator training and console knobs documented; add runtime alerts for reservoir_free < 10% and kernel OOM spikes
monitoring_playbook: Dashboards: reservoir_free per GPU, kv_eviction_rate, admission_decisions by reason, microbatch_size distribution
Alerts: sustained reservoir_free < 5% for 1 minute, admission_degrade_rate > 2% sustained, kernel_oom_count > 0 in 5m
Runbook steps: 1) throttle incoming traffic at ingress, 2) increase reservoir_target_pct by +10, 3) enable extra eviction slack or increase quantized-degrade ratio
Post-incident: capture heap profile, KV usage snapshot, and microbatch histograms; open postmortem if kernel OOM occurred
risks_mitigation: Risk: Affinity misclassification causes elevated latency for important traffic — Mitigation: conservative default thresholds and an opt-out tag for customer-critical routes
Risk: Reservoir conservative sizing reduces throughput — Mitigation: auto-tune reservoir_target based on steady-state latency and utilization signals
Risk: Added CPU overhead on worker hot path — Mitigation: microbench affinity scorer and implement inlined fast path with fallback to sampled scoring
Risk: Cross-worker coordination inconsistencies — Mitigation: keep local decisions primary; use cluster signals only for long-term trending
